approved: Moved the second reading of Appropriation Bill (No. 3) 2013-2014, seeking just under $11.6 billion in additional funding including an $8.8 billion one-off grant to the Reserve Bank and almost $750 million for the Department of Immigration and Border Protection.

Moved the second reading of Appropriation Bill (No. 4) 2013-2014, seeking just over $3.2 billion including almost $2.2 billion for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and almost $400 million for offshore asylum seeker management.

Moved a second reading amendment noting the government's own Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook revealed a $17 billion budget blow-out, 60 per cent of which was due to its own decisions. Said Australia's economy rose from the 15th to the 12th largest in the world under Labor, and questioned the Treasurer's $9 billion grant to the Reserve Bank, for which no evidence of a formal request had been produced.

Contrasted the government's $17.7 billion deficit with Labor's independently audited projection of a $4.2 billion surplus by 2016-17, and said 63,000 full-time jobs had been lost under the government, or about 350 a day. Highlighted youth unemployment of 16.5 per cent in the Illawarra, well above the state average of 11.8 per cent, and criticised cuts to trade training centres and Better Futures employment programs.

Criticised Labor's handling of the Tourle Street Bridge, which will now cost more than $100 million to add two lanes that would have cost $15 million if built originally. Highlighted RAAF Base Williamtown, which directly employs over 3,500 people and injects more than $280 million in salaries into the Hunter region, and said boat arrivals had fallen by more than 80 per cent since the election.

Criticised the government for revoking $10 million in funding to transform Junction Oval into a hub for Cricket Victoria, including national headquarters for women's and Indigenous cricket. Disputed Minister Brandis's claim that Labor cut arts funding, noting the Creative Australia policy delivered $235 million in new arts investment, including $75 million for the Australia Council.

Argued that the ABC's programming and funding decisions lack transparency, citing producer Chris Hetherington's rejected $30,000-per-episode series pitch and a Paul Keating interview series with Kerry O'Brien that could generate over $1 million in production funding, amid a review of the $1.4 billion ABC and SBS budget.

Argued that the government's own $14.8 billion appropriation bills expose the hypocrisy of its 'budget emergency' claims, turning a projected $4.2 billion surplus for 2016-17 into a $17.7 billion deficit, including an unjustified $8.8 billion appropriation for the Reserve Bank and $400 million in cuts to public hospitals.

Opposed the government's freeze of $11.5 million in Building Multicultural Communities Program funding, including an $85,000 grant to the Ted Noffs Foundation's Randwick drug and alcohol program, and criticised the undermining of the Gonski education reforms and the prospect of a Medicare co-payment.

Criticised the government's $8.8 billion transfer to the Reserve Bank Reserve Fund as a politically timed manoeuvre to pad this year's deficit before receiving a dividend back around August 2014, at an interest cost of about $400 million a year, and condemned the $11.5 million cut to the Building Multicultural Communities Program, which withdrew $22,000 promised to the Filipino-Australian Society of the Hunter Valley and about $100,000 to Vedic Samiti Newcastle.
Spoke in favour of the government's appropriation bills for 2013 to 2014 and against the opposition's amendment, responding to remarks from the member for Chifley.

Supported the appropriation bills, citing net government debt of about $200 billion with $123 billion in additional forecast deficits, warning of $667 billion in debt within a decade if unaddressed, and said the government has approved about $400 billion worth of held-up projects while planning to repeal more than 8,000 regulations.

Detailed a $13.2 million cut to the health portfolio including funding for the 48-year-old Alcohol and Other Drugs Council of Australia, established in 1966, saving about $1.5 million annually against an estimated $15 million lifetime cost of just one case of foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, and said only two of 29 ACT community groups awarded multicultural grants have been paid amid an $11.5 million program cut.

Argued for developing northern Australia with strong scientific baseline data, noting only five of Queensland's 25 major river systems currently have that baseline research, and criticised the previous government for sending equipment repairs 3,000 kilometres to Bandiana in Victoria instead of using local Townsville engineering firms.

Noted the appropriation bills seek just under $11.6 billion in additional spending, including an $8.8 billion grant to the Reserve Bank that formed a significant part of the government's budget deficit blow-out. Said 63,300 full-time jobs had been lost across the economy in the six months since the government was elected.

Detailed election commitments delivered in her Solomon electorate, including $150 million for stage 1 of the Palmerston Regional Hospital, comprising a $110 million Commonwealth contribution and $40 million from the Northern Territory government. Highlighted $70 million for the duplication of 12 kilometres of Tiger Brennan Drive and $300,000 for a CCTV rollout in Darwin and Palmerston crime hot spots.

Cited Clean Energy Regulator figures showing the carbon tax was a $7.6 billion hit on the economy in its first year, directly affecting around 75,000 businesses, while emissions barely changed by 0.1 per cent. Also noted the bills include an $8.8 billion one-off grant to the Reserve Bank to strengthen its financial position.

Criticised the government for announcing $210 million for roads in the Leichhardt electorate while ignoring the Gove community, whose population is set to fall from 4,000 to 1,200 after Rio Tinto's bauxite refinery closure. Said a $900 million cut to university funding would cost Batchelor Institute and Charles Darwin University $900,000 over four years, affecting 2,163 students.

Supported the Appropriation Bills, welcoming a needs-based drought relief package replacing the old exceptional circumstances boundaries, and said Labor turned a $20 billion cash surplus into net debt of more than $200 billion, costing $10 billion a year in interest.

Supported the Appropriation Bills, criticising Labor's wasteful spending, and recalled the Treasurer's budget night claim on 8 May 2012 of delivering a promised surplus despite no real structural budget repair, citing a colleague's dismissal of $250,000 in savings as insignificant.

Criticised the government's approach as a form of economic austerity likened to 1930s liquidationist thinking, arguing the Prime Minister's handling of Holden and Qantas reflected callous indifference that would have worsened unemployment during the financial crisis.

Criticised the appropriation bills for cutting $4.8 million from education, $13.2 million from health, $4.6 million from legal policy advocacy and $11.5 million from the Building Multicultural Communities Program, and said the leaked Commission of Audit report criticised the Prime Minister's paid parental leave scheme, which would cost an estimated $5.5 billion, as unfair compared with the existing scheme already covering 95 per cent of women.

Detailed Tasmania's economic decline under 16 years of Labor and four years of Labor-Green coalition government, citing an unemployment rate of 7.6 per cent against a 5.8 per cent national average, youth unemployment as high as 20 per cent, total state debt approaching $3.9 billion, an unfunded superannuation liability of $6.2 billion, and 287 nurses sacked in nine months, and urged Tasmanians to elect Will Hodgman's Liberals on 15 March.

Supported the appropriation bills totalling nearly $15 billion, including an $8.8 billion grant to rebuild the Reserve Bank's capital buffer after Labor withdrew $5.23 billion from it in 2009-10, highlighted Eagleby in his Forde electorate as home to Queensland's four most disadvantaged streets with 12 per cent unemployment, and announced close to $1 million for CCTV cameras and $3 million toward revitalising the Beenleigh Town Centre.
